**Source:** Hegde, D. V., Kim, T. K., Pogorelov, N. V., Jones, S. I., & Arge, C. N. *Ensemble Modeling of the Solar Wind Flow with Boundary Conditions Governed by Synchronic Photospheric Magnetograms. I. Multi-point Validation in the Inner Heliosphere*. *The Astrophysical Journal* (arXiv:2505.22386v1, accepted May 27, 2025).

**Density and temperature at the inner boundary (Section II.4, "MHD Boundary Conditions")**

The paper says: "We establish the SW density and temperature at the inner boundary by assuming momentum flux and thermal pressure equilibrium, as given by ad hoc prescriptions" followed by the two relations:

- N·V_R² = N_min·V_fast²
- N·T = N_min·T_max

where N is density (cm⁻³), V_R is radial velocity (km/s), and T is temperature (10⁶ K).

**Reference values (Section II.4):**
- N_min = 200 cm⁻³
- T_max = 2×10⁶ K
- V_fast = 700 km/s
- Minimum SW velocity set to 200 km/s

**Magnetic field (Section II.4):** The WSA radial field is scaled by a factor the text gives as "22" (likely a rendering of 2, to correct the open-flux underestimate at 1 AU). The paper also reduces WSA velocities by 75 km/s and sets B_θ = 0, with B_φ = −ΩR·B_R·sinθ / V_R.

**Inner boundary radius:** Section II.1 gives the default inner boundary as R = 0.1 au (21.5 R⊙). Section II.4 says the boundary was moved to 19 R⊙ during P6 and P7 ("we adjust the inner boundary to 19"), and kept at 21.5 R⊙ for P8 and P9.

**Model:** The paper uses MS-FLUKSS, an MHD model, coupled with the WSA coronal model (Section I: "coupled with the semi-empirical WSA coronal model"). It does not use ENLIL or EUHFORIA. Those appear only as other mixed models cited in the introduction.

The search turned up the ENLIL calibration rules for the inner boundary, but no single CCMC page that spells out the full derivation of density and temperature from momentum flux and thermal pressure.

- **Calibration approach:** Odstrcil's CCMC workshop slides say WSA speeds need recalibration at the inner boundary, because the solar wind expansion depends on coronal temperature, the ratio of specific heats, and the initial speed. Parameters at Earth depend on the coronal temperature, ratio of specific heats, and on initial speed. ENLIL needs to use re-calibrated WSA solar wind flow speeds at the inner boundary.
- **Fast-stream parameters and balance rules:** A 2012 CCMC workshop deck lists the fast-stream inputs (number density, mean temperature, specific heat ratio, alpha fraction) and the balance rules used to set the rest. It names momentum flux balance: NVX (x = 2) and pressure balance (Pthe = const). This matches the momentum-flux and thermal-pressure logic you asked about.
- **Conflicting default values:** The same 2012 deck gives different fast-stream values by inner-boundary choice. For WSA at 0.1 AU, it lists density 200 cm⁻³ and temperature 1.0 MK; for MAS at 0.14 AU, 100 cm⁻³ and 0.6 MK. An older 2007 deck gives 300 cm⁻³ and 1 MK. Check the version you are using before relying on any single number.
- **Parameter names in the documentation:** A CCMC parameter-listing slide names the inputs as fast-stream radial velocity, number density, temperature, radial magnetic field, specific heat ratio, alpha fraction, and an exponent for N·V, with the exponent set to 1 or 2 depending on whether thermal or total pressure is held constant. =1 (=2) if Pthe (Ptot ) = const
- **Cone-model density:** For CME clouds, a 2015 paper notes that the cloud density is a free parameter, by default 4 times larger than typical mean values in the ambient fast wind, and the cloud temperature is set equal to the ambient fast-wind temperature.

I did not find the current CCMC model-documentation page or Odstrcil's 2003 paper, so the exact current formulas are not confirmed here. The CCMC ENLIL options page and Odstrcil (2003) are the places to check for the definitive equations.

Properties of stream interaction regions at Earth and Mars during
the declining phase of SC 24
Paul Geyer1, Manuela Temmer1, Jingnan Guo2, 3, and Stephan G. Heinemann1, 4
1 University of Graz, Institute of Physics, Austria
2 School of Earth and Space Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei, PR China
3 CAS Center for Excellence in Comparative Planetology, Hefei, PR China
4 Max-Planck-Institut für Sonnensystemforschung, Justus-von-Liebig-Weg 3, 37077 Göttingen, Germany
February 12, 2021
ABSTRACT
Aims. We inspect the evolution of stream interaction regions (SIRs) from Earth to Mars, covering the distance range 1–1.5 AU, over
the declining phase of solar cycle 24 (2014–2018). So far, studies only analyzed SIRs measured at Earth and Mars at diﬀerent times.
We compare existing catalogs for both heliospheric distances and arrive at a clean dataset for the identical time range. This allows a
well-sampled statistical analysis and for the opposition phases of the planets an in-depth analysis of SIRs as they evolve with distance.
Methods. We use in-situ solar wind data from OMNI and the Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN) spacecraft as
well as remote sensing data from Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). A superposed epoch analysis is performed for bulk speed,
proton density, temperature, magnetic ﬁeld magnitude and total perpendicular pressure. Additionally, a study of events during the two
opposition phases of Earth and Mars in the years 2016 and 2018 is conducted. SIR related coronal holes with their area as well as
their latitudinal and longitudinal extent are extracted and correlated to the maximum bulk speed and duration of the corresponding
high speed solar wind streams following the stream interaction regions.
Results. We ﬁnd that while the entire solar wind high speed stream shows no expansion as it evolves from Earth to Mars, the crest
of the high speed stream proﬁle broadens by about 17%, and the magnetic ﬁeld and total pressure by about 45% around the stream
interface. The diﬀerence between the maximum and minimum values in the normalized superposed proﬁles increases slightly or
stagnates from 1–1.5 AU for all parameters, except for the temperature. A sharp drop at zero epoch time is observed in the superposed
proﬁles for the magnetic ﬁeld strength at both heliospheric distances. The two opposition phases reveal similar correlations of in-situ
data with coronal hole parameters for both planets. Maximum solar wind speed has a stronger dependence on the latitudinal extent of
the respective coronal hole than on its longitudinal extent. We arrive at an occurrence rate of fast forward shocks three times as high
at Mars than at Earth.
Key words. Sun: solar wind – Sun: heliosphere – Sun: solar-terrestrial relations
1. Introduction
Solar wind (SW) high speed streams (HSS) emanate from coro-
nal holes (CHs) on the Sun and form with the ambient slow
solar wind so-called stream interaction regions (SIRs). As CHs
are rather long-lived structures, SIRs can be observed over sev-
eral rotations and are then called co-rotating interaction re-
gions (CIRs). SIR/CIR structures are detected at various loca-
tions in the inner heliosphere by in-situ instruments, showing
typical characteristics. As the fast SW (with speeds as high as
800 kms−1) compresses the slow portion (about 400 kms−1),
density and interplanetary magnetic ﬁeld (IMF) magnitude are
rapidly enhanced (see e.g., Schwenn 2006). The density ﬁnds
its maximum just before the total perpendicular pressure has its
peak (slow SW changes to fast SW regime) which is commonly
referred to as the stream interface (SI) (e.g., Jian et al. 2006). The
fast SW propagates freely with its characteristic high speed in
the rarefaction region following the SIR. CIRs and SIRs may de-
velop forward or reverse shocks (or both) as they expand through
the heliosphere (e.g., Jian et al. 2006; Huang et al. 2019).
The formation of shocks can be explained using simple 1-D
modeling (e.g Hundhausen 1973): as the crest of the pressure
wave moves faster than the front decelerated by the slow SW
ahead, the wave steepens. Eventually, this steepening evolves
into a sharp, discrete boundary at the front and rear of the wave,
thus forming shocks. Hence, the further out in the heliosphere
the higher the occurrence rate of both kinds of shocks, due to
further steepening as observed when comparing SIRs at 0.3 AU
